Hi,

my first guess would be an issue with the input data object and/or coordinate names; you could try letting inlabru construct the integration by itself, with
  like(..., samplers = boundary, domain = list(coordinates = mesh))
instead of manually supplying ips to see if that makes a difference.
Also, consider the 'include' argument to `like` to tell it which model component are needed by each likelihood; it might be that it's trying to evaluate a model component using data that doesn't allow it to do that (but you're supplying the same data object in both cases, so any issues with that would be due to the integration points)

Otherwise, I may need a complete reproducible code&data example to run here for debugging.
(A small subset of the data would be good; can be simulated, as long as it produces the same error on your system)

Finn

parts:
Hi,

I had to change the mesh construction to a more reasonable size to debug this, but have found the main cause of the problem, which is a bug in how it handles "missing" data, which in this case means model components that are used by only one of the two likelihoods. The intended solution to this problem is to use the include/exclude arguments to like(), an if the models had been purely linear, this would work:
lik1 <- like("cp",

formula = coordinates ~ .,
             data = data,
             ips = ips,
             include = c("point_field", "Inter_point"),

)
lik2 <- like("normal",

formula = size_ha ~ .
             data = data,
             exclude = c("Inter_point"))

Unfortunately, the point_field*scaling term of the second predictor of your model means one has to specify the full expression in the formula, and then the bug is again triggered, in the second INLA iteration.
I'm not yet sure why the bug is triggered in the second step but not the first, so I need to debug some more to find out.

Fortunately, there is a (partly better) alternative, which is to use the INLA "copy" feature to implement the point_field*scaling term.
Use the following model specification:

cmp =
  ~ -1 +
point_field(coordinates, model = matern) +
mark_field(coordinates, model = matern) +

Inter_point(1) + Inter_mark(1) +
  point_field_copy(copy = "point_field", fixed = FALSE) +

DC+GDP+density+total+rural+agriculture+industry +services +forest

lik1 <- like("cp",

formula = coordinates ~ .,
             data = data,
             ips = ips,
             include = c("point_field", "Inter_point"),

)
lik2 <- like("normal",

formula = size_ha ~ .,
             data = data,
             exclude = c("point_field", "Inter_point"))

I've attached the full working code, including my modified mesh code suggestion that extends the mesh beyond the coastlines and artificial country borders, but sets up the likelihood only on the country bounded domain, just as before.
The mesh has far fewer nodes, making the inference take about 20 seconds, so you could still increase the resolution if you prefer.

Finn

Hi again,

I got confused earlier; the problem with the predict() call is that you're supplying only a grid of coordinates (masked by the boundary), which is enough to predict the spatial fields, but to predict the given expression across space, you also need to supply the covariate values for all those grid points.
The error message in this case comes when it tries to evaluate the "density" covariate and doesn't find it in the data set, and therefore ends up (due to R features...) finding the _function_ called density, and gets a NULL result. Before it gets to this point, it also tries to evaluate the DC and GDP covariates, but since their names don't appear anywhere at all, they get replaced by 1, for backwards compatibility reasons (I'm looking for a way to make this an error in a safe way, to make it easier to spot this kind of problem).
So the error wasn't quite the same as the one as before, and it was instead a problem with the input data to predict().

Finn

Hi,

I had to change the mesh construction to a more reasonable size to debug this, but have found the main cause of the problem, which is a bug in how it handles "missing" data, which in this case means model components that are used by only one of the two likelihoods. The intended solution to this problem is to use the include/exclude arguments to like(), an if the models had been purely linear, this would work:

lik1 <- like("cp",
             formula = coordinates ~ .,
             data = data,
             ips = ips,
             include = c("point_field", "Inter_point"),

             )
lik2 <- like("normal",
             formula = size_ha ~ .
             data = data,
             exclude = c("Inter_point"))

Unfortunately, the point_field*scaling term of the second predictor of your model means one has to specify the full expression in the formula, and then the bug is again triggered, in the second INLA iteration.
I'm not yet sure why the bug is triggered in the second step but not the first, so I need to debug some more to find out.

Fortunately, there is a (partly better) alternative, which is to use the INLA "copy" feature to implement the point_field*scaling term.
Use the following model specification:

cmp =
  ~ -1 +

  point_field(coordinates, model = matern) +
  mark_field(coordinates, model = matern) +
  Inter_point(1) + Inter_mark(1) +
  point_field_copy(copy = "point_field", fixed = FALSE) +

  DC+GDP+density+total+rural+agriculture+industry +services +forest

lik1 <- like("cp",
             formula = coordinates ~ .,
             data = data,
             ips = ips,
             include = c("point_field", "Inter_point"),

             )
lik2 <- like("normal",
             formula = size_ha ~ .,
             data = data,
             exclude = c("point_field", "Inter_point"))

I've attached the full working code, including my modified mesh code suggestion that extends the mesh beyond the coastlines and artificial country borders, but sets up the likelihood only on the country bounded domain, just as before.
The mesh has far fewer nodes, making the inference take about 20 seconds, so you could still increase the resolution if you prefer.

Finn

             data = data,

  point_field_copy(copy = "point_field", fixed = FALSE) +

             data = data,
             ips = ips,
             include = c("point_field", "Inter_point"),

lik2 <- like("normal",
             formula = size_ha ~ .,
             data = data,
             exclude = c("point_field", "Inter_point"))

Finn
